children: and its creditors are discussing a debt transaction that could extend upcoming maturities, raise new capital and give some unsecured bondholders a stronger position in the company’s capital structure.

Under the proposal, holders of Jeld-Wen’s first-lien loan due in 2028 could extend their debt at face value or receive repayment at a discount, Bloomberg News reported, citing people familiar with the discussions. New capital would help fund those repayments and add liquidity to the window and door maker’s balance sheet.
The plan also could allow unsecured bondholders that provide fresh money to obtain first-lien status, putting them alongside existing secured term-loan lenders in the repayment hierarchy.

Creditor groups have hired advisers as discussions continue. First-lien lenders are working with Moelis & Co. and Gibson Dunn & Crutcher. Unsecured bondholders have retained Houlihan Lokey and Davis Polk & Wardwell. Jeld-Wen is working with Evercore.

The talks come as building-products companies contend with weak construction demand and elevated borrowing costs. Jeld-Wen’s second-quarter revenue slipped 0.7% from a year earlier to $817.8 million. The company reported a $31.5 million net loss.
Management said in August that market demand remained weak, although the rate of decline was starting to ease.
reported $1.25 billion in total debt at the end of the second quarter. Its debt prices have improved as investors have become less concerned about a potential restructuring.

The company’s $400 million of unsecured notes due in December 2027 recently traded around 90 cents on the dollar, compared with 61.5 cents in early April. Its $374 million term loan was quoted around 87 cents, up from 75.25 cents in April.
Jeld-Wen has said its refinancing efforts are focused on protecting liquidity and financial flexibility while giving the business more time to improve as construction markets stabilize.

title: Jeld-Wen creditors are said to discuss debt extension, fresh capital
